birthday.note: Robert's first declaration of love in the very first letter, the seed of everything that follows.
Elizabeth's grateful reply, opening the exchange that would become the whole correspondence.
Robert's promise of spring and a meeting, one of the first expressions of his determined pursuit.
Elizabeth's first reference to her health and seclusion, establishing the physical distance between them.
Robert's quiet devotion — wanting few friends and seeing her week to week — showing the deepening bond.
Robert's response to Elizabeth's confession of her brother's death, marking a new depth of shared trust.
Robert's declaration that his whole life is wound up in her, from the period when love was openly avowed.
Robert's tender wish that the beam of the light will reach her, from the days of the ring and hair.
Robert's anticipation of Tuesday, their day, from the Christmas season when their bond was sealed.
Robert's cry to marry soon and end all the secrecy, from the spring when plans became urgent.
Robert's awe at Elizabeth and his willingness to follow her anywhere, from the early summer.
Elizabeth's reflection on their first meeting and how she never guessed she would love him, a callback to the beginning.
Elizabeth's declaration that she is wholly his, from the tense weeks before their secret marriage.
Elizabeth's final letter, asking him to pray for her on the eve of their elopement, closing the story.

anniversary.note: Robert’s first letter declares love for her books and for her, setting the correspondence in motion.
He follows the first letter with an even plainer avowal that he loves her too.
He writes of spring and says he will surely see her, turning hope into a promise.
After months of letters and visits, he names their bond as friendship forever.
He answers her confidence with gratitude and the idea that loving her is better than happiness.
Elizabeth answers with the first full surrender of herself to him in everything but harm.
Robert writes of being wound around her and living only with reference to her.
Elizabeth sends a ring whose colour echoes his blue flowers, a private token.
Robert declares himself wedded to her now, moving from friendship to marriage.
He names being with her as his only good in the world.
Elizabeth recalls his early chestnut-tree image, a callback to their first year.
Robert remembers that his first words to her were 'I love you,' echoing the beginning.
He writes that his love would outlast any separation or accident.
Elizabeth exults in the irrevocability of giving herself to him.

thank you.note: Robert's opening letter shows the wholehearted admiration for Elizabeth's poems that started their correspondence.
He immediately pairs praise of her books with love for her, a bold early declaration.
Elizabeth's reply expresses deep gratitude and establishes the mutual warmth of their exchange.
Elizabeth's vivid praise of Robert's poem shows her close, discerning engagement with his work.
She promises never to forget the feelings he has shared with her, marking their growing intimacy.
Robert's confession of having once been untrue to her underscores how seriously he takes their bond.
Elizabeth's striking reaction to Luria conveys how powerfully Robert's new work affected her.
Robert's tender promise to kiss her back to his heart captures his deepening devotion.
Her reflection on how little time they have known each other highlights the intensity of their connection.
Elizabeth's distress over losing Flush is a private, recognizable moment of their shared life.
Robert's grateful thanks after their secret marriage express his joy and appreciation.
Elizabeth's farewell before their departure shows her looking ahead to having only him to love her.

sorry.note: Robert's early declaration that he loves her work and her.
Elizabeth wonders if Robert truly regrets the lost chance to meet her.
Robert speaks of the friendship Elizabeth offers becoming sure.
Elizabeth asks for plainness and freedom from ceremony between them.
Robert is glad and thankful that Elizabeth's first outing went well.
Elizabeth says she will never forget these things nor remember them more coldly.
Robert blesses Elizabeth for what she has been and will be to him.
Elizabeth struggles to answer Robert's declaration and thanks him from her heart.
Robert says his whole life is wound around Elizabeth.
Elizabeth protests that she never meant harm by speaking of kindness.
Robert says every word Elizabeth writes goes to his heart and lives there.
Elizabeth says Robert is to her instead of all, not merely a crowning happiness.
Robert asks Elizabeth's forgiveness for his foolish letter and warmth.
Elizabeth says she owes Robert the only happiness of her life.

missing you.note: Robert's early open declaration of love, setting the whole correspondence in motion.
Elizabeth answers the fear of burdening him, establishing their ease in letters.
Robert's hopeful promise of spring and finally seeing her, carrying the early longing.
Elizabeth's playful callback to Spiridion, showing their shared literary memory.
Robert's confession of one earlier untruth to her, deepening their honesty.
Elizabeth's vivid, breathless reaction to Luria, marking their creative partnership.
Elizabeth's wonder at Robert's love for her, central to their emotional turning point.
Robert's intimate invitation to know him through Landor's verses and his own heart.
Elizabeth's callback to the chestnut tree, recalling Robert's earlier image.
Robert's gentle reassurance about his sister's visit and their shared private world.
Robert's playful praise of Elizabeth's good sense, keeping their private teasing alive.
Elizabeth's refusal to say yesterday's foolishness, preserving their tender private understanding.

farewell.note: Robert's first love-letter to Elizabeth, setting the whole story in motion.
Elizabeth's grateful first reply, the answering voice that began it all.
Robert's promise to see her in spring, the first turning of hope toward meeting.
Robert telling Elizabeth he would rather lose her letters and even her sight than harm her, the first declaration of self-sacrifice.
Elizabeth's heartbreaking memory of her brother's last promise before his death, the wound she finally entrusted to him.
Robert's submission to her refusal of Pisa, the moment of patient faith.
Robert's words of complete surrender, 'my whole life is wound up and down and over you,' the love now declared.
Elizabeth's postscript about the ring and the hair, the first giving of herself.
Robert's New Year's love-song, 'this love I bear you,' naming it love for the first time.
Elizabeth's final letter before the elopement, 'It is dreadful to have to give pain here by a voluntary act,' the cost of their leaving.
Robert's farewell letter before the wedding, 'You have given me the highest, completest proof of love that ever one human being gave another.'
Elizabeth's last words to him, 'Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?' — the close of the correspondence.
